changes.after: With &&, C checks the left side first. If it is false, C skips the right side.

before: A zero scalar value is false in a condition; a nonzero value is true. Logical operators produce int 0 or 1.
&& evaluates its right operand only if its left operand is true. || skips the right operand when the left is true.
denominator !=0 must come before the division in this expression. A false left side prevents division by zero.
& and | operate on integer bits and do not provide the same short-circuit guard as && and ||.
Expected output or behavior: 1. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Try a zero and a nonzero denominator, explaining which operands execute before computing the result. You may trace it without a C compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: In these number conditions, 0 means false and a nonzero value means true. The logical operators `&&`, `||`, and `!` give a result of 0 or 1.

`&&` means both conditions must be true. If its left side is false, C skips the right side. `||` means at least one must be true; it skips the right side when the left is true. This skipping is called short-circuiting.
The denominator is the number you divide by. Check `denominator != 0` before the division. If it is zero, the left side is false and the division is skipped.
`&` and `|` work on individual bits of integers. They do not skip the right side like `&&` and `||`. Use the double signs for this guard.
The denominator is 2, so the first check passes. 8 divided by 2 is 4, which is greater than 2. Both checks are true, so accepted prints as 1.
Set the denominator to 0. Follow the left check first and decide whether the division is reached.
